articles.title_orig: Padres make quick work of Cubs to sweep Wild Card Series
articles.title_zh: Padres make quick work of Cubs to sweep Wild Card Series
articles.content_orig:
SAN DIEGO -- The Padres spent September as the hottest team in baseball, surging into the postseason and securing a Wild Card Series at Petco Park. Gavin Sheets , meanwhile, spent most of the month in a walking boot.
All summer, Sheets had been playing through a nasty injury -- a plantar plate tear in his left foot. He wondered if he’d be able to contribute at all. The Padres decided there was almost no way that Sheets could contribute defensively. He’ll probably require surgery at some point this offseason.
But maybe … just maybe … if Sheets could heal just enough … he could deliver a meaningful swing or two in the postseason.
Sheets came off the bench to deliver the swing that broke the Cubs in Game 2 of the National League Wild Card Series on Wednesday night -- a pinch-hit, two-run home run that sent Petco Park into delirium and the Padres on course for Milwaukee.
With their 4-1 victory over the Cubs, San Diego secured a trip to the NL Division Series against the Brewers, beginning on Saturday night. Milwaukee finished with the Majors’ best record and has Jacob Misiorowski lined up for Game 1.
A tall task, sure. But the way these Padres are playing right now, would you put it past them?
They made quick work of the Cubs this week, dispatching them in two games that were never really all that close. The two teams played 18 innings at Petco Park this week. The Padres led after 17 of them -- sweet revenge after their 2025 season came to an end with a Wild Card Series exit at Wrigley Field.
In Game 1, the Padres were a force of nature . The ballpark partied from the very first pitch (a Michael King fastball past Pete Crow-Armstrong) to the very last pitch (Joe Musgrove punctuating his triumphant return to the mound with a game-ending strikeout). They won, 8-0.
Game 2 brought a different kind of postseason energy. A party, to be sure. But one with some tension mixed in. October baseball, on the final day of September.
San Diego jumped in front in the second with Xander Bogaerts’ RBI single and Ethan Salas’ sacrifice fly. (Salas, the youngest player in history to catch a postseason game, also became the youngest player at any position with a postseason sac fly -- since at least 1954 when that stat was fully tracked.)
But the Cubs scratched a run back against Nick Pivetta in the fourth and worked their way into the Padres’ bullpen. Crow-Armstrong and the top of the lineup loomed in the fifth.
There were two outs and a runner aboard, and Chicago manager Craig Counsell had gone with right-hander Daniel Palencia. Sheets strode to the on-deck circle, then, eventually, the batter’s box -- with those three familiar thuds echoing through the Petco Park sound system.
This was the moment they’d been planning for. The moment they’d been hoping for. When Sheets is right, he mashes right-handed pitching. He’s a weapon in the clutch and a force off the bench.
As it turned out, Sheets would take all of one plate appearance across two games in the series. One swing, even.
He made it count. Palencia threw a 100.8 mph fastball at the bottom of the zone on the inner half. Sheets turned on it -- the hardest pitch any Padre has ever homered on, regular or postseason.
Petco Park exploded and Sheets trotted around the bases. The Padres led, 4-1. Their lockdown bullpen could take it from there -- straight to Milwaukee.

articles.title_zh: Red Sox vs. Yankees live updates, news, starting pitchers for Game 2: Sonny Gray, Max Fried take the mound Wednesday
articles.content_orig:
The New York Yankees have advanced to the American League Division Series. Convincingly.
For the second straight game, the club made its rivalry with the Boston Red Sox look far from competitive, winning Game 2 of their wild-card series 9-2 to finish off a sweep. The Yankees will face another AL East foe, the Tampa Bay Rays , in the next round.
The Yankees did this without Aaron Judge , whose health still looms over the Bronx . Game 1 of the ALDS is scheduled for Saturday at 6:30 p.m. ET.
Wednesday's wild-card Game 2 started as a duel between starting pitchers Max Fried and Sonny Gray but turned into a rout gradually and then suddenly. First came a Luis García Jr. homer to break a scoreless tie in the fourth inning. Cody Bellinger doubled the New York lead in the fifth with an RBI single, right after the Red Sox opted to pull Gray.
Then came the sixth inning.
It began hopefully for the Red Sox, who scored their first run of the series on a Willson Contreras homer that might or might not have received some help from a fan . Either way, Contreras and Fried exchanged hard stares during a long home run trot. Game on, right? Right?
Boston's next lever to pull was bringing in ace Garrett Crochet for his first appearance since April, returning from shoulder inflammation and a lat strain. It was a nice story, one that was soon ruined by Crochet failing to get any of his four batters out. He exited with his team down by two runs, with the bases loaded and no outs.
The Red Sox brought in setup man Garrett Whitlock to try to keep the game competitive, but productive outs scored two more runs. Boston then intentionally walked Ben Rice to set up a faceoff between Whitlock and Bellinger.
Bellinger made that decision look foolish.
Everything that followed was merely procedural for a lopsided Yankees win.
The Red Sox made themselves a playoff team after a start so bad they fired manager Alex Cora, and they could do no wrong for one magical stretch in the middle of the season. However, there was once again a clear talent deficit against the Yankees, even without Judge.
This is the second straight year that Boston has ended its season in New York, though the Sox at least played a Game 3 last season. This time around, they were outscored 18-2. The Yankees' two starting pitchers, Fried and presumptive Cy Young winner Cam Schlittler , combined to throw 12 1/3 innings with 5 hits and 1 run allowed, with 16 strikeouts.
The Red Sox had injuries, of course, their most recent being Roman Anthony in Game 1 . And it's not like we can pretend they had the fully functional version of Crochet. Still, this result begs the question of what the plan is under chief baseball officer Craig Breslow , who has appeared to steer the club into the exact kind of tier MLB teams want to avoid in the long term.
Yankees fans haven't exactly been thrilled with their team's recent era, either, but they at least get to watch their team play this weekend, with the hope of benefiting from a chaotic American League field this season. New York gets two full days of rest before its series opener against the Rays, against whom they went 6-7 in the regular season.
Follow along with Yahoo Sports for live updates, highlights and more as the New York Yankees host the Boston Red Sox in Game 2 of the AL wild-card round on Wednesday.
This one is over. For a second straight game, the Yankees were all over the Red Sox, and now they will head to Florida to face another AL East foe, the Tampa Bay Rays.
Boston's season, which ranged from turbulent to thrilling, is over.
Aroldis Chapman strikes out the side in the bottom of the eighth inning. He remains a tough pitcher to face.
The Red Sox have one more inning to make up for a seven-run deficit, so they can force a Game 3, so they can fly to Florida and face the Rays on Saturday.
Austin Wells knocks in another run, and that will do it for Garrett Whitlock. Carry on.
Warren has no further trouble and the Yankees are two innings away from a date with the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.
Nick Sogard gets a run back with a line drive homer to right field off Will Warren.
Spencer Jones strikes out to end the inning. All the Red Sox need to do now is octuple their runs scored this series to force extra innings.
Cody Bellinger, whose dad, Clay, threw out the first pitch today, blows this game wide open with a three-run homer. The Red Sox intentionally walked Ben Rice into an empty first base, and Bellinger just made that blow up in their face.
A sacrifice bunt ends up just foul for Ryan McMahon, who then delivers a swinging bunt to score on a fielder's choice. And now an intentional walk of Ben Rice for Whitlock to face Cody Bellinger.
Wells hits a sacrifice fly to left and Jazz Chisholm Jr. takes third. This inning has been a slow motion crash for Boston.
Crochet's first appearance in five months didn't go too well. The Yankees now have the bases loaded with no outs, so the Red Sox pull their returning ace for Garrett Whitlock. He'll face Austin Wells as the Yankees threaten to blow this game wide open.
Spencer Jones reached first on a dropped third strike (thanks to an overturned call), stole second, took third on a bad throw to second and scored on a George Lombard Jr. single. The Yankees pull a run out of basically nothing to go back up two runs.
Fried gets out of the inning and in comes Red Sox ace Garrett Crochet to pitch the seventh.
The last time Crochet pitched for Boston, Alex Cora was manager.
Max Fried was a strike away from making it six scoreless innings, but Willson Contreras clubs a high fastball to right field, and a fan catches it. Replay review finds no fan interference, and Boston has its first run of the series.

articles.title_orig: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike taken to hospital after attempted execution, lawyer says
articles.title_zh: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike taken to hospital after attempted execution, lawyer says
articles.content_orig:
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has been taken to hospital after her heart was still beating following two lethal injections during her execution, her lawyer says.
Her legal team filed an emergency motion to halt the convicted murderer's execution as it was happening, saying: "Ms Pike has lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat and is audibly snoring."
One of her attorneys told the BBC that Pike, 50, was "being provided life-saving measures" in hospital after two syringes of pentobarbital had been administered.
Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
Slemmer's mother May Martinez said she wanted the execution to take place, telling the Associated Press on Saturday: "Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run."
Her attempted execution took place at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville at about 20:00 local time on Wednesday night.
Pike was given two doses of pentobarbital, and the curtain in the witness room was closed twice, the Associated Press reports.
Media were at some point asked to leave, the news agency said.
Pike's legal team said in a statement to the Tennessean newspaper: "Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution.
"We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy."
Pike's lawyers filed an emergency motion to stay her execution and provide medical care after the lethal injection was apparently botched.
District Judge Clifton L Corker issued a ruling noting that "medical personnel have begun to administer medical care as requested in the motion".
The Tennessee Department of Correction has said it stands by all the actions it took during the attempted execution.
"The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General's Office," department spokesperson Dorinda Carter told the Tennessean newspaper.
"The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility," she said.
Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine who told the BBC he had been retained by Pike's legal team as a medical expert, said she likely never achieved a sufficient blood level of pentobarbital to cause apnoea and cardiovascular failure during the attempted execution.
"It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury," Zivot said in an email.
The attempted capital punishment went ahead after multiple last-minute legal challenges by Pike's lawyers failed.
The US Supreme Court had thwarted two separate efforts to stop the lethal injection.
Late on Wednesday, the Supreme Court overturned a reprieve granted by a lower court earlier in the day, which granted a pause saying it needed more time to consider the arguments in Pike's case.
It followed the Supreme Court's earlier dismissal of an appeal by Pike's lawyers, who had argued the jury did not get the chance to weigh mitigating evidence of Pike's documented history of childhood sexual abuse, before they sentenced her to death in 1996.
The defence said that for years, the state of Tennessee had argued in court that she lied about being sexually abused as a child.
But at a recent hearing about her execution method, the state said it did not dispute that she had suffered sexual abuse and rape.
Tennessee's governor denied a clemency request this week from Pike, the only woman on the state's death row.
May Martinez, mother of Colleen Slemmer, outside a court hearing in 2006
In her clemency petition, Pike said that she intended to beat Slemmer, not kill her, but that she was unable to "put the brakes on".
"I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid," she said in a statement. "It took me numerous years to even realise the gravity of what I'd done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime."
The murder in 1995 created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee, after Colleen was found with an inverted pentagram - a symbol that is associated with satanic groups - carved into her chest. Pike has denied carving the symbol herself.
Before the killing, Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her then-boyfriend.
Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.
Colleen's mother May Martinez said she had waited decades to see Pike's sentence carried out.
Over the weekend, she told the Associated Press that a group helped raise funds for her and her husband to travel from Florida to Tennessee to witness the execution.
"Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst," Martinez said.
Since 1976, when the Supreme Court resumed the death penalty, only 18 women have been executed in the US, compared to 1,663 men. That's about 1% of all US executions.

articles.title_orig: Steelers trade Joey Porter Jr. to the Cowboys
articles.title_zh: Steelers trade Joey Porter Jr. to the Cowboys
articles.content_orig:
Last year, once the Cowboys realized that linebacker Micah Parsons wasn’t going to play without a new contract, Dallas traded him.
This year, the Steelers apparently have realized that cornerback Joey Porter Jr. wouldn’t be playing without a new contract. And so they’re trading him.
Per multiple reports, the Steelers are sending Porter to the Cowboys.
The full terms have yet to emerge. The separate question will be whether the Cowboys will give Porter the contract he couldn’t get in Pittsburgh.
Dallas could decide to ride it out in 2026, with Porter making $3.924 million. Then, they could apply the franchise tag in 2027.
It’s hard to imagine the Cowboys tradining for a player who apparently doesn’t intend to play until he gets a new deal.
The common link between Porter, a second-round pick in 2023, and Parsons is that both are represented by David Mulugheta of Athletes First. Mulugheta also represents receiver George Pickens, who was traded by the Steelers to the Cowboys in May 2025.
The Cowboys haven’t given Pickens a new deal. For 2026, they tagged him. For receivers, the franchise tender is well below market value. It is for cornerbacks, too.
Much will be revealed in the coming hours. For now, the most important point is that the impasse between the Steelers and Porter has ended with Porter being sent to a new team.

Published: 20:44 EDT, 30 September 2026 | Updated: 22:04 EDT, 30 September 2026
Sean ' Diddy ' Combs is reportedly being sent back to solitary confinement at FCI Fort Dix prison in New Jersey , following claims about his VIP treatment inside .
The disgraced hip-hop mogul, 56, is returning to solitary in response to a recent NBC News report about the alleged special treatment he's been receiving from inmates willing to do his bidding – from cooking, cleaning to even offering massages.
Sources told TMZ it is the standard procedure for an inmate while prison officials conduct an investigation.
The rapper was previously put in solitary confinement back in July after getting into a fight with another inmate.
In the new NBC report, one inmate claimed Diddy has access to a cell phone where he receives nude photos from a former girlfriend as well as a 'jail broken' tablet that he's used to watch his archnemesis 50 Cent's damning documentary about him.
Diddy's representative Juda S Engelmayer told the Daily Mail about the recent reports: 'There is no way we can independently verify those rumors.'

Four men who spent time in Diddy's unit opened up to the publication about his allegedly luxurious lifestyle – revealing how the music mogul has been living it up during his years-long prison sentence.
According to the insiders, Diddy enjoyed premium liquor smuggled in by guards, has purchased a mood-boosting antidepressant from inmates and has fellow prisoners store his fan mail and phone for him.
One inmate provides him with Chinese-style massages.
Maintaining such a lifestyle doesn't come cheap; Diddy apparently splashes thousands of dollars a month to continue enjoying the luxury prison lifestyle.
The funding apparently comes from prisoners who work for Diddy, who have their commissary accounts replenished from people on the outside.
Photos obtained by the publication show the meals prepared by inmates specifically for him and others  – pizza and a plate of meat with rice.
'This is not some normal s*** you see in jail. This is some rich s***,' according to one of the men.
In response to the article, Engelmayer told The Daily Mail: 'The continued scrutiny of every mundane detail of Sean Combs's life in prison has reached the point where the media characterizes ordinary prison life as news.'
'The only real news is that Sean continues to serve his sentence within the rules and he patiently awaits the court's decision on his appeal.'

During Combs's trial, his ex-girlfriend Cassie Ventura delivered graphic testimony, alleging that the music mogul abused her over more than a decade.
The once Hollywood power player endured a major fall from grace after Cassie accused him of rape and repeated physical abuse in a bombshell $30 million lawsuit that was quickly settled – and prompted others to come forward with claims.
But now, it seems he has been embraced by prisoners.
'He’s a billionaire. People are in awe of him,' one source said. 'Money is power, especially behind bars.'
In addition to the various luxuries he has allegedly been enjoying, he has apparently been online as well.
Thanks to a 'jailbroken' tablet he somehow retrieved, Diddy has been watching movies and documentaries – including 50 Cent's Sean Combs: The Reckoning – and scrolling on Instagram on a cell phone.

The report alleges Diddy has purchased Remeron, an antidepressant known for being a mood booster and one that is prescribed to inmates struggling with depression and anxiety.
Nicknamed 'rem-roms' by prisoners, the medication is also available in the prison's black market, a source said.
Inmates have also taught Diddy the ropes; in the early days of his sentence, he was allegedly seen wearing just a towel or boxer shorts after a shower, sparking inmates to issue him a warning about how the minimal clothing would make him a target for sex.
A representative for the Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP) said they were unable to comment on Diddy 'for privacy, safety, and security reasons' when reached for comment.
'For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including whether a particular individual is the subject of allegations, investigations, or sanctions,' the BOP's Office of Public Affairs told The Daily Mail.

'Like all correctional agencies, contraband, particularly cell phones, narcotics, and weapons, remains a constant challenge, and we continue to tackle the problem of contraband being introduced into our facilities. 'We are fully committed to safeguarding everyone in our custody and to maintaining the safety and security of our correctional staff and surrounding communities. To this end, we operate under a controlled environment that is both secure and humane.'
'Additionally, based on the need to ensure safety and security in our institutions and in accordance with privacy concerns, we do not discuss potential allegations of staff misconduct, nor do we confirm or deny the existence of a corresponding investigation.'

articles.title_orig: In photos: China's Xi hardens Taiwan warning as country celebrates week-long National Day holiday
articles.title_zh: In photos: China's Xi hardens Taiwan warning as country celebrates week-long National Day holiday
articles.content_orig:
China began its seven-day National Day holiday on Thursday after President Xi Jinping used his annual opening speech to sharpen Beijing's message on Taiwan.
Speaking at the Great Hall of the People on Wednesday, on the eve of the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China, Xi said Beijing must " resolutely crack down on 'Taiwan independence' separatist forces, oppose interference from external forces" and "advance the great cause of national reunification."
The language is harder than in Xi's speech last year, when he said Beijing "firmly opposes" independence activities .
The shift comes days after Xi's state visit to Washington, where he urged President Donald Trump to outright "oppose" Taiwan independence, and to limit Washington's support for the self-ruled island that Beijing claims its own. That wording would be stronger than the longstanding U.S. position of not supporting Taiwan independence.
"It has been speculated for more than a year that Xi would do this, but it was the first time we saw him do it," said Allan von Mehren, China economist at Danske Bank.
The Trump administration paused a $14 billion Taiwan arms package in May and has struck a less supportive tone toward the island over the past year.
State leaders, including Xi, presented flower baskets at the Monument to the People's Heroes in Tiananmen Square on Wednesday, the country's Martyrs' Day, a day before National Day. Xi walked around the monument in tribute to fallen national heroes, according to photos published by state media .
Crowds in Beijing gathered on Thursday morning to watch the People's Liberation Army honor guard escort the national flag to Tian'anmen Square, with a military band playing the national anthem and thousands of doves released into the sky.
Travelers and city workers are heading out for the holiday, which runs from Thursday through next Wednesday. Workers often stretch the break to 13 days, by taking leave from Monday to Wednesday, spanning the Mid-Autumn Festival on Friday.
China's Ministry of Transport projects about 2.13 billion trips over the holiday week, or roughly 300 million a day.
Daily border crossings are forecast to average about 2.16 million. Bookings for domestic flights over 2,000 kilometers are up about 14%, and international ticket bookings are up 22.5% from a year earlier, according to official figures .
Golden Week is typically a gauge of domestic consumption, but years of subdued consumer demand mean heavy travel may not translate into bigger spending. Trip volumes and revenue rose during last year's holiday but remained around 3% lower than in 2019 before the pandemic, according to Goldman Sachs.
The authorities in Hong Kong expect 7.4 million passenger trips in and out of the city over the upcoming week, and Macau anticipates more than 5 million trips during the holiday.
At a celebration event in Hong Kong on Tuesday, Chief Executive John Lee said the city's first five-year plan would help it "share the rhythm of China's growth."

articles.title_orig: Becerra and Hilton clash over taxes, AI and immigration during the CNN California governor debate
articles.title_zh: Becerra and Hilton clash over taxes, AI and immigration during the CNN California governor debate
articles.content_orig:
Democratic governor sharply critical of Donald Trump for not passing comprehensive federal AI regulations
Governor Gavin Newsom signed laws Wednesday aimed at protecting California workers from the threats of artificial intelligence , including potential job losses and workplace surveillance.
The laws ban employers from using the technology to predict a worker’s emotional state by using their biometric data, require employers to send written notices to workers if AI is responsible for mass layoffs and ban employers from relying on AI to decide to fire someone.
The Democratic governor also signed an executive order to require state agencies to continue to refer to the technology as “artificial intelligence” instead of the term “super intelligence” as Donald Trump recently ordered US diplomats to use.
“AI should expand opportunity – not come at the expense of workers and families,” Newsom said in a statement. “As this technology reshapes the workplace, California is putting people at the center.”
He sharply criticized Trump at an hour-long event with reporters Wednesday for not passing comprehensive federal AI regulations at a time when industry leaders are warning about the technology’s risks. Trump said Tuesday that top tech leaders signed a voluntary accord to “self-police” AI development.
The governor signed a law this month requiring operators of AI chatbots to perform risk assessments before rolling them out and an executive order requiring the state to consult with experts to further improve oversight over the industry.
“We have to do a lot more in the absence of federal leadership,” Newsom said, leaving the door open for the possibility of calling lawmakers back for a special session to further tackle the issue.
The news conference came on Newsom’s last day to sign or veto bills before he terms out in January. He started the event by signing a law creating a tax credit program aimed at helping local news organizations – including newspapers, digital outlets and TV stations – hire and retain journalists. Newsom criticized what he called Trump’s assault on a free press, pointing to the president’s barring of news organizations from the White House.
Newsom also spoke about the upcoming midterms, which will decide control of Congress. He involved himself early in that fight by leading Democrats last year in a redistricting battle to improve their chances of winning more House seats. He’s said repeatedly that the stakes are high if his party doesn’t succeed in November.
“There will not be a free and fair election in 2028 unless we take back the House of Representatives,” he said Wednesday.
Asked if he had set a deadline for himself to decide to run for president in 2028, Newsom hedged, saying: “That moment will arrive when it arrives.”
Former Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris, who, like Newsom, hails from the San Francisco Bay Area, has also said she’s considering running for the job in 2028. Newsom told CNN recently that he would not run for president if she entered the race. He said the two have not spoken since that interview aired.
Newsom weighed in on a proposal to temporarily raise taxes on billionaires that will be on the ballot in November, which he’s consistently opposed. He said he respects supporters of the measure, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who are committed to addressing income inequality in the country.
“He’s spot on about the balance between the rich and the poor,” Newsom said. “On this issue, we fundamentally disagree.”
Newsom’s remarks came hours before a gubernatorial debate between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton.
“You’re going to ask me, ‘Are you going to watch the debate?’” he said. “No.”

Two Australian citizens were onboard a flight to Tel Aviv that was diverted after one of the pilots allegedly stabbed the other in an attack , according to the Israeli embassy.
The passengers are a Jewish couple from Sydney, the embassy in Australia confirmed to the Guardian on Thursday. No further details were provided.
The flydubai aircraft was travelling from the United Arab Emirates to Israel when it was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
One of the pilots, whom Israeli officials said was an Omani citizen, is accused of stabbing his co-pilot. During the alleged attack, the plane plunged about 17,000 feet in just two minutes .
Passenger Yaniv Hayoun later recounted how he and other passengers heard screaming and felt pressure as the plane dived before forcing their way into the cockpit and finding the attacker at the instrument panel.
“I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during a meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel. “He was trying to destroy the instruments to disable the plane.”
Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, said the incident reminded him of the 11 September attacks.
“You have here a very special incident, and due to the real heroism of some people on board, they were saved.”
Newman said heightened security alerts had been issued following the attack.
“It just shows that … those that hate Israel also hate the peace.
“It’s an attempt to hit at the peace itself, at the Abraham Accords, and the relationships which Israel does have with Arab and Muslim countries.”
The Abraham Accords normalised relations between the UAE and Israel in 2020.
Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said it was too early to tell who was ultimately behind the the incident.
There are about 12,000 Australian citizens living in Israel and 25,000 in the UAE.

articles.title_orig: Switzerland’s glaciers are losing an astonishing amount of ice. See the meltdown.
articles.title_zh: Switzerland’s glaciers are losing an astonishing amount of ice. See the meltdown.
articles.content_orig:
The front of Morteratsch Glacier in south-east Switzerland, which has been attacked by warm air and water
Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.
More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary".
They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.
The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.
There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed.
But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.
The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting.
Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be "extreme". This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear.
"It's really just disastrous," said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report.
Swiss glaciers started the summer in an already difficult place, covered by less snow than usual after a mild winter.
And much of that snow disappeared quickly in the early and intense heatwaves of May and June , exposing the glacier ice below.
Bare ice is darker and less reflective than fresh snow, so absorbs more of the Sun's energy.
That left glaciers vulnerable to melting even faster in subsequent heatwaves.
"Ten years ago, I wouldn't have thought that it's possible to lose glaciers so quickly," said Dr Fabien Maussion, a glaciologist at the University of Bristol, who was not involved in the Swiss report.
"What's happened over the summer now is extremely distressingâ¦ but at the same time it was to be expected from a climate scientist's perspective," he added.
Meltwater from glaciers can be an important source of water for irrigation, hydropower and even shipping traffic during hot, dry conditions.
Scientists estimate that Swiss glaciers released 2.2 trillion litres of meltwater between July and September.
Although that helped to ease water shortages this summer, it has rapidly diminished the frozen supply.
The loss of ice could pose long-term challenges, Huss warned, with smaller glaciers unable to top up water levels to the same extent.
"Every drop of water that runs off during these heatwaves is kind of old water that's been stocked in the glacier ice centuries or decades ago," said Huss.
"It's helping us [now] but it's unsustainable, so we won't have it at [our] disposal in the next heatwave."
The River Rhine reached record lows in places this summer , affecting shipping navigation routes and increasing transport costs.
One of the most ominous findings is what researchers observed at measurement sites at the highest elevations, where temperatures are lowest and glaciers are typically snow-covered.
Even as high as 3,500 metres above sea level, scientists found no snow remaining at the end of summer.
"At some glaciers we've seen four metres of ice loss at the highest point, where they should be covered by several metres of winter snow at this time of the year," said Huss, from Glacier Monitoring Switzerland.
Snow is like glacier food - and under stable conditions some of it would eventually compact into ice.
But if no snow survives the summer, it cannot replace the ice lost to melting at lower, warmer elevations. The glacier will starve, shrink and eventually disappear.
"Glaciers are complex because they gain mass at the top and they flow downstream, so there is a lot of physics," explained Maussion.
"But in its simplest form, what we see right now is that we took an ice cube out of the fridge and it's just melting in front of our eyes."
Scientists say the climate is now too warm for many Alpine glaciers to survive.
Some, like Plattalva in eastern Switzerland, have already disappeared.
But researchers stress that sharp cuts to carbon emissions can still save much of the world's glacier ice.
This is particularly the case for the Himalayas and the polar regions, where most of the planet's ice resides.
"There we still can make a big difference with protecting the climate," said Huss.
"If these ice masses can be saved or stabilised, we can limit the rise of global sea levelsâ¦ which could affect billions of people living along the coast."

An immigration judge has cleared the way for the leader of Wisconsin’s largest mosque, an outspoken advocate of Palestinian rights, to be deported on the grounds that he is a threat to national security.
Salah Sarsour was detained in Milwaukee in March by ICE officers . A federal judge ordered Sarsour’s release in June, saying he raised a “substantial” claim that the Trump administration was targeting him for speaking out against Israel and advocating for Palestinian rights.
Sarsour said in a statement on Wednesday that the immigration judge’s ruling was “deeply disappointing,” but that he intends to appeal.
“I will continue fighting to defend the right to free speech and to stay in the country I have called home for more than three decades,” Sarsour said.
The government says Sarsour's decades-old terrorism convictions in Israel make him a threat to national security in the U.S. and accuse him of lying about it on his green card application. Immigration Judge Jayme Salinardi agreed but tossed out the claim that Sarsour lied on his green card application.
Sarsour, who was born in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, was imprisoned in Israel in 1988 after confessing to throwing a Molotov cocktail and stones at Israeli military personnel. In 1995, he was convicted of attempting to hold weapons and ammunition. Sarsour denies committing those crimes. His attorneys say he was tortured and coerced into confessing in both instances.
Sarsour does not have a criminal record in the U.S., where he has lived since 1993. His attorneys say the U.S. government has known about Sarsour’s convictions in Israel since he arrived. He is president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee.
Deportation to the West Bank, “means the end of my life,” Sarsour told The Associated Press in a Tuesday interview. One of his attorneys, Patrick Taurel, told the AP that Sarsour’s earlier treatment by Israeli authorities is “probably a good indicator of what awaits him” if he is deported.
At a status hearing Wednesday, Taurel pressed the judge to specify that Sarsour can only be deported to Israel and the Palestinian territories. Jordan, a country with which Sarsour has no connection, is listed as a possible destination on the deportation order.
Sarsour was instructed by immigration officers to list Jordan as his home country on an immigration form because his preferred entry — “Palestine” — is not a fully independent, unified state. But he “has no right to reside in Jordan,” attorney Patrick Taurel said.
“That issue is preserved on appeal,” he said.
Taurel said on Wednesday that Sarsour is being unfairly targeted.
“If Salah can be deported for his speech in support of Palestinian rights, anyone can face the same fate,” Taurel said.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a rare memo in June 2025 saying Sarsour could be deported on the same grounds as Mahmoud Khalil and Mohsen Mahdawi, both advocates for Palestinian rights whom the Trump administration has tried to expel, according to court documents.
Before the judge’s ruling, Taurel said Sarsour would fight his removal and would likely need to demonstrate that he would face torture by Israel if he were deported.
“It’s a very high bar, although I think we can meet it in this case, given what Salah has already experienced, and given the government of Israel’s treatment of people similarly situated” to him,” Taurel said.
Appeals in Sarsour's case are due in 30 days. Salinardi did not schedule a future court date on Wednesday, and announced he is retiring and that Judge Craig Defoe will oversee the case going forward.
Jawad Boulos, who represented Sarsour when he was convicted in Israel, testified in August that Sarsour was coerced into confessing and that he wasn’t convicted of any charge tying him to a terrorist organization.
Boulos also testified that Sarsour was tortured while in the custody of the Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency. The Department of Homeland Security questioned Boulos about the torture allegations, questioning how he could know it was true.
Sarsour’s current defense team has asked why U.S. authorities waited until this year to detain him. Taurel said the government has known about Sarsour’s time behind bars in Israel for decades and that Sarsour never concealed that information from U.S. immigration authorities.
Experts on forced confessions and the treatment of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli prisons also testified in Sarsour’s defense. Israeli military courts have faced repeated scrutiny over allegations of limited due process and the high conviction rate of Palestinians. Israel rejects the claims.
In June, U.S. District Judge James Patrick Hanlon ordered Sarsour released from custody pending his immigration case. Hanlon found Sarsour could have a case arguing the U.S. government was retaliating in violation of his free speech rights and that attorneys for ICE and DHS had not explained why Sarsour was suddenly considered a threat after decades of legal residency.
The Trump administration has appealed Hanlon’s decision to release Sarsour from ICE detention.
Sarsour, who has Type 2 diabetes, lost more than 30 pounds (14 kilograms) while detained by ICE, and his blood sugar levels were checked only once a month, putting him at risk of organ failure or death, his attorneys said.
An investigation by KFF Health News and The Associated Press found that hundreds of detainees in at least 33 states have filed federal lawsuits with similar allegations of medical neglect.
Sarsour is among several people who have been arrested in the U.S. and threatened with deportation after speaking out in favor of Palestinians since the start of the Israel-Hamas war in October 2023.

articles.title_orig: MI5 warns UK universities over ‘theft of tech secrets by Chinese front company’
articles.title_zh: MI5 warns UK universities over ‘theft of tech secrets by Chinese front company’
articles.content_orig:
Security service says academics should stop working with and taking grants from firm backed by Chinese intelligence
MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities
MI5 has issued a rare public warning to UK universities that China’s intelligence service is using a front company to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects.
Britain’s domestic security service said researchers and academics should cease work with the China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI), sometimes also known as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT).
MI5 believes the body poses a “significant threat” and is now prepared to say publicly that the CGTRI is a front for Chinese intelligence, namely the Chinese ministry of state security (MSS). It said continued collaboration by UK academics could be prosecuted under the National Security Act 2023.
The Chinese organisation has funded 100 or more academics at a string of universities across the UK, in return for access to the research, which it is alleged found its way back to China’s intelligence service.
On Wednesday, the Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”. A spokesperson said: “We firmly oppose such baseless allegations and have lodged solemn representations with the UK side.
“Exchanges and collaboration between UK universities and China have always been conducted on a voluntary basis and in compliance with laws and regulations. Such exchanges and collaboration are mutually beneficial.”
The MI5 warning sent a shock wave through the UK university sector, with staff reviewing the implications for existing or future partnerships with China, and experts raising concerns about the rigour of the vetting process in sensitive research collaborations.
Areas of research targeted include AI, cybersecurity, covert communications and steganography – the embedding of secret data in seemingly innocuous files. MI5 believes it has clear evidence of sensitive information being passed back to Chinese intelligence, and the Guardian understands that some British-based academics were given honours and awards by the Chinese as well as research money.
Successive British governments have courted Chinese investment and encouraged academic cooperation. Sam Dunning, the director of the UK-China Transparency group, said: “It is reasonably obvious from the internet that CGTRI was focused on areas of high interest to the military and intelligence services.
“Granted, CGTRI used various aliases and have certainly obscured some funding streams, but as for the UK universities or academics who knew they were dealing with CGTRI, open-source research made clear that CGTRI had military or intelligence links.”
Vice-chancellors who spoke to the Guardian said they were not aware of receiving any funding from the Chinese institute, but warned that individual academics working on joint projects with other universities or third parties may not know the original sources of funding.
Prof Peter Mathieson, vice-chancellor of the University of Edinburgh and the lead for international security for Universities UK, which represents 142 institutions across the UK, said MI5’s warning meant that future collaborations with the CGTRI would be illegal.
“They are saying that anyone who has a link to this institute up until now has not committed any kind of offence, because it’s not previously been said this was a high-risk activity.
“Now that they have said it, we have to sit up and take notice. It’s very much a forward-looking directive.
He added: “I can’t speak for MI5, but I think what they are attempting to say is that people may not realise that the institute they are working with is connected to the security services of the Beijing government. And there’s no reason why anyone should have realised that, because it’s a new piece of information that MI5 has discovered.”
In the alert issued on Wednesday, the Security Service said: “MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage.”
It said that CGTRI had “very strong ties to the … MSS, China’s civilian intelligence and security service”.
The alert continued: “Many academic institutions and individuals will to date have engaged with CGTRI in good faith given CGTRI’s obfuscated links to MSS.
after newsletter promotion
“UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions. Further, academics are advised to establish the ultimate funding source when conducting any research collaboration with Chinese institutions, to ensure CGTRI is not involved.”
That MI5 has decided on a public alert as a deterrence strategy, rather than trying to pursue every single case, demonstrates the scale of Chinese state espionage targeting the UK. It hopes universities will heed the warning and immediately cease their work with CGTRI.
The Guardian understands that cutting-edge British research on scraping social media (gathering large amounts of information from social sites and apps) is among the data to which MI5 believes Chinese intelligence gained access.
The security minister, Dan Jarvis, demanded universities end ties to the CGTRI. He said: “This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security and that of our allies.
“I have written to all university vice-chancellors to ensure they support their staff to end all arrangements with this company, preventing further benefit to the Chinese intelligence services and ensuring compliance with the National Security Act.”
Responding to the MI5 alert, Vivienne Stern, the chief executive of Universities UK, said universities took their responsibilities around research security and national security extremely seriously.
“The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes, while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation,” she said.
Chinese government filings suggest that CAGT is connected to the China General Technology Group, a major state-owned conglomerate administered directly by the government of China that is also known as Genertec .
The Genertec brand has a UK presence, with a company called Genertec (UK) Ltd, appearing to be owned by the Chinese state.
The British company, which has been registered in the UK for a decade and is based in a shared office address on Southwark Bridge Road, had £5.6m in the bank according to accounts to the end of 2024 – cash that seems to have come exclusively from a single property transaction.

Backpack has officially been crowned the chunky champion of Fat Bear Week after an intense competition with Bear 910.
Officials at Alaska ’s Katmai National Park and Preserve, where over a dozen brown bears competed to be named the heaviest, announced the winner Tuesday night.
“We have a new fat Bear Champ! Bear 89 nicknamed ‘Backpack,’” park officials wrote on Facebook.
Backpack won the finals with 103,334 votes compared to Bear 910’s 98,253 votes, according to explore.org , whose nature cameras captured the Fat Bear Week contestants.
“Your votes, your posts, your favorite bear campaigns, and your shared love for Katmai’s wild places turned this week into a collective story shaped by thousands of voices,” the park officials said. “It’s a reminder that just like America’s 250th anniversary, traditions endure because people keep them alive.”
The competition, currently in its 12th year, honors the resilience of the 2,200 brown bears living in the preserve along the Alaska Peninsula, which stretches from the southwest region of the state toward the Aleutian Islands.
Established in 2014, Fat Bear Week is an interactive initiative to educate the public about coastal brown bears, the close relatives of grizzlies.
Chunk — officially recognized as Bear 32 — won last year’s title at an estimated 1,200 pounds. He was knocked out during the first round of this year’s competition by Bucky, who later lost a direct faceoff to Backpack.
A total of 16 bears entered this year's single-elimination, bracket-style tournament to compete for the heavyweight crown.
"Fat bears are successful bears," explore.org explains on its website. The animals gorge on the abundant salmon that return to the Brooks River beginning in late June. It is along the river that they build up the vital fat reserves required to survive winter hibernation. To be included in the tournament, bears must frequently visit the river area.
In midsummer, adult male brown bears generally weigh between 600 and 900 pounds. By the time hibernation approaches, following months of feeding on migrating and spawning salmon, large males can weigh significantly more than 1,000 pounds.
Female brown bears are approximately one-third smaller. Bears may consume as many as 30 fish each day during this time of year, working relentlessly to eat a year’s worth of food in approximately six months.
During their winter hibernation, the bears go without eating or drinking and lose a third of their overall body weight.
Contenders in Fat Bear Week also included five bear families, reflecting the record number of families and cubs present at the river this summer.
A mother bear must feed and protect her young while consuming sufficient calories to sustain herself through hibernation. Cubs frequently face the danger of attacks by other bears because of territorial behavior or food scarcity.
Bear 132 and her three spring cubs successfully reached the semifinals, but ultimately lost to Bear 910.
Contestant profiles identify Bear 132 as one of the largest and most experienced mother bears at Brooks River. In mid-July, one of her cubs became separated from the family for several days and roamed the river corridor alone. They were reunited a short time later.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced on Wednesday that he had directed the U.S. military to cut 20% of the number of general roles.
The new reduction, which Hegseth revealed during an address at the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia on Wednesday afternoon, doubles the already 10% cuts to general and flag officer positions that Hegseth instructed the military to make last year.
According to Fox News , which previously reported Hegseth's intention to announce the cuts, military services are being ordered to finish making the reductions by Jan. 1, 2027. The network reported that some of the affected roles are expected to be downgraded, rather than cut entirely.
During his speech on Wednesday, Hegseth did not specify a timeline for the cuts, but said that “the number crunchers say we’ve fired 10% of the generals and admirals across the force, and that number sounds about right.”
“And I know—because I directed it—that we’ve also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10%,” Hegseth said. “So yes, 20% reduction across the board.”
“Now, the media calls that a purge,” he continued. “I call it accountability, and long overdue, and frankly, the bare minimum. As usual, what the media levels as an accusation, I wear as an accomplishment. You see, you can’t change a culture with the same people who enabled it.”
Peter Feaver, a professor of political science at Duke University and a specialist in civil-military relations, says that many experts agree “that there probably could be a trimming of the general and flag officer ranks, that they had grown perhaps unnecessarily large in recent years, and that some rebalancing would be prudent if it was done carefully and managed carefully.”
“In the abstract, could the U.S. military absorb a 20% cut in general flag officer ranks if properly managed? I’d say yes, and I think most experts would say yes,” Feaver says.
He notes, though, that the 20% reduction also comes after additional cuts to the military’s top ranks, and on a relatively fast timeline.
“The burden will be on Secretary Hegseth and his team to demonstrate that they are making these cuts wisely and consolidating wisely and not recklessly,” Feaver says. “The faster they do it, and the less explanation that they give, and the more that really good officers are cut, the more doubt there will be.”
During his speech, Hegseth referenced an address he gave in Quantico, Virginia last year, in which he outlined his vision for the Department of Defense. Last year’s speech, he said on Wednesday, “reestablished a singular mission for this department: warfighting. Preparing to fight and preparing to win. Unrelenting, unapologetic, and uncompromising in that single pursuit.”
“Now, I think the generals heard the message,” he continued. “Those who responded positively, which is most of them, are leading newly focused and newly empowered and disciplined formations. Those generals who did not, who clung to the ‘woke’ department or seemed to think civilian control of the military is simply a suggestion—well, they no longer work here.”
Hegseth’s speech comes at a time of turmoil within the military’s leadership: At least 20 military and civilian leaders have been pushed out or resigned since Hegseth was sworn in as Defense Secretary. In 2025, Hegseth told the active duty military to cut 20% of its four-star general officers and the National Guard to cut 20% of its top officials. It is not known if all of those reductions have been completed.
Hegseth said in a memo at the time that the reduction plan would eliminate “redundant force structure to optimize and streamline leadership” and that the goal was to prevent “unnecessary bureaucratic layers” within the military, The Associated Press reported .
“This is not a slash-and-burn exercise meant to punish high-ranking officers,” Hegseth said in May 2025. “This has been a deliberative process, working with the Joint Chiefs of Staff with one goal: maximizing strategic readiness and operational effectiveness by making prudent reductions in the general and flag officer ranks.”
Hegseth has faced a wave of backlash from Democrats and some Republicans over his management of the Department of Defense, in addition to his handling of other issues, such as the war in Iran. Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, who has clashed with the Trump Administration on multiple occasions since President Donald Trump returned to the Oval Office, introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth earlier this month, including allegations regarding the Iran war.
Before that, Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina publicly criticized Hegseth’s management of the agency, after Dan Driscoll resigned as Army Secretary amid reports of tension between him and Hegseth.
“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis said in a social media post . “I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it.”
The Defense Secretary also unveiled a slew of new initiatives on Wednesday, including something called “Project Meridian,” which he said would be “an effort led by America’s best minds to study the future of warfare,” including “discovering, developing, and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes … on any future battlefield, from under the Earth to beyond the Moon.” Hegseth said that Elon Musk, who previously served as one of President Donald Trump’s top advisers before their very public feud last year, along with former Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey, will co-lead the initiative.
Hegseth also announced that the Department of Defense plans to build “the next great American base.” He lamented that a new military base hadn’t been constructed within the U.S. in decades, and called on governors to “bring us their best sales pitch.”
“If your state wants the honor of hosting 15 to 25,000 of America’s great troops, show us why and how you’re going to do it,” he said.
During his speech, Hegseth applauded his efforts to eliminate what he called “woke” culture within the American military , such as rolling back diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives.
“The only focus, as you know, in your formations should be training, readiness, accountability, discipline, and lethality. And when you pursue those things, you don’t have to walk on eggshells,” Hegseth said. “The complainers, the ideologues, and the poor performers are no longer in the driver’s seat. No more silly PowerPoint trainings or drag queen shows. No more diversity quotas. No more gender pronouns. No more identity months. Only the warrior ethos.”
“We are no longer the ‘woke’ department or the weak department,” he said. He went on to use derogatory terms to refer to people who are overweight and people who are transgender.
“No wimps, no radicals,” he said. “Just warriors. Just tough, ready, committed troops.”

articles.title_orig: Opinion | How China became the world’s gold superpower
articles.title_zh: Opinion | How China became the world’s gold superpower
articles.content_orig:
Beijing built its dominance through innovation and meticulous planning, not superior natural reserves
Perhaps no story illustrates the secret of China’s industrial success better than its rise as the world’s gold superpower.
China has revered the metal for millennia, yet it has never had a gold-based economy. Its own deposits were simply too scarce.
In 1975, as China began its economic modernisation, it desperately needed gold to fund reform and build up foreign reserves. Despite its best efforts, it produced a meagre 13.8 metric tons a year. South Africa, then the undisputed king of gold, produced many times that. Canada, the United States and Australia each comfortably outproduced China as well.

articles.title_orig: Sean Combs’ release date is pushed up, as new report details pampered prison lifestyle
articles.title_zh: Sean Combs’ release date is pushed up, as new report details pampered prison lifestyle
articles.content_orig:
Inside the walls of Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey, no one is living quite like inmate #37452-054.
There are men who cook for him and men who clean for him. There are men who make his bed and men who do his laundry. There is even a man who gives him Chinese-style massages.
This is how Sean “Diddy” Combs has been living in prison, according to four men who have spent time in the same unit as the disgraced hip-hop mogul. They were granted anonymity to speak freely about life inside the prison.
“This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” said one of the men. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.”
This story is also drawn in part from photos and videos taken inside the prison and reviewed by NBC News. They include footage of Combs appearing to use a contraband phone.
Diddy appears to use cellphone in prison
Combs, 56, is serving a 50-month sentence for prostitution-related offenses. But he is still living a privileged life, the sources said, and it’s not just because of the inmates willing to perform even the most basic tasks for him for the right price.
Multiple sources said he uses contraband cellphones to scroll Instagram and scan nude and sexually explicit photos that an old girlfriend sends him. He’s been able to buy from other inmates an antidepressant drug sought out for its mood-boosting effects — Remeron, or “rem-roms” as they are known in prison. On weekend nights, he’d often tap into a secret stash of premium liquor, which would be smuggled in by guards and shared with a tight group of fellow inmates.
“Hell yeah, I drank with him,” said one of the men, who recounted drinking Hennessy with Combs.
A spokesperson for Combs downplayed the details of his prison life.
“The continued scrutiny of every mundane detail of Sean Combs’s life in prison has reached the point where the media characterizes ordinary prison life as news,” the spokesperson said. “The only real news is that Sean continues to serve his sentence while awaiting the court’s decision on his appeal.”
A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson said the agency does not comment on a particular inmate’s conditions due to “privacy, safety and security reasons.”
“Like all correctional agencies, contraband, particularly cell phones, narcotics, and weapons, remains a constant challenge, and we continue to tackle the problem of contraband being introduced into our facilities,” the spokesperson added in a statement.
Combs’ exalted existence behind bars doesn’t come cheap.
He has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his lifestyle to the low-security prison, sources said, with the money flowing from people outside prison to the commissary accounts of those inmates performing services for him.
Those paid by Combs include a man who would clean the toilet and shower areas before he’d use them, and men who would secretly cook him special meals — curry chicken, pizza, empanadas — using a makeshift heating element submerged in water, sources said.
“After a while, I got tired of cooking,” said one man who described preparing meals for Combs and other inmates. “He started going to the Jamaicans.”
There are also inmates who hold on to Combs’ phone and fan mail for him.
“It’s so much that he gets,” one of the sources said. “He doesn’t have room for it.”
Like many other state and federal prisons across the U.S., Fort Dix has grappled with a contraband problem . Just last week, five people, including a current and former corrections officer, were charged with running a scheme to smuggle illicit items into the South Jersey prison. The contraband included knives, marijuana and cellphones, federal prosecutors said.
Since 2020, authorities have also charged multiple people for allegedly using drones to drop illicit goods into the Fort Dix prison yard or atop a roof . The suspects have included inmates and outside accomplices who had previously served time at the facility. In one case, Fort Dix staff intercepted a 46-pound laundry bag filled with contraband.
Combs isn’t the first famous person to receive special treatment behind bars. Harvey Weinstein, for one, was held in a private room at the Rikers Island jail in New York, with access to his own phone, bathroom and television, according to The City Reporter .
The massive Fort Dix prison, 60 miles southwest of New York City, houses about 4,000 inmates.
Combs arrived there in October following his conviction on two counts of transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters.
The trial featured lurid testimony about highly choreographed sexual encounters Combs organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers, elaborate costumes, drugs and former girlfriends — including the singer Cassie — who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.)
His trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.
Following his sentencing, Combs’ lawyers pushed for him to be sent to Fort Dix in part because it offers a drug treatment program. Completing the monthslong program often leads to a reduction of an inmate’s prison term, making it highly coveted.
Combs entered the program upon his arrival at Fort Dix. Sources said it took little time for him to acquire a phone, alcohol and a growing number of inmates on his payroll.
“Pretty much the day he arrived, the party started,” one of the sources said.
Many Fort Dix inmates consume alcohol and Remeron, sources said. The medication is prescribed to inmates suffering from depression and anxiety. But it’s also bought and sold on the prison’s robust black market, the sources said.
“You can pretty much get anything except a key to the front door and a female,” one of the sources said.
Among the items Combs has gotten his hands on, two sources said, is a “jailbroken” tablet that he has used to watch movies and documentaries — including “Sean Combs: The Reckoning,” the Netflix docuseries produced by his longtime nemesis 50 Cent.
His presence at the prison has also led to some surreal moments, the sources said. In his first few days, he would walk around in only a towel or boxer shorts after a shower, prompting inmates to warn him that he could be targeted for sex.
“That’s not normal,” one of the sources said.
Over the summer Combs was placed in solitary confinement following a fight with another inmate, NBC News reported in July . He was later kicked out of the drug treatment program, sources said.
But after he was moved out of solitary, the sources said, he went right back to living the life great wealth can buy you in prison, with a team of inmates catering to him.
“He’s a billionaire. People are in awe of him,” said one of the sources. “Money is power, especially behind bars.”
Rich Schapiro is a reporter with the NBC News national security unit.
Chloe Melas is an entertainment correspondent for NBC News.

Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.
More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary".
They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.
The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.
There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed.
But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.
The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting.
Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be "extreme". This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear.
"It's really just disastrous," said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report.
Swiss glaciers started the summer in an already difficult place, covered by less snow than usual after a mild winter.
And much of that snow disappeared quickly in the early and intense heatwaves of May and June , exposing the glacier ice below.
Bare ice is darker and less reflective than fresh snow, so absorbs more of the Sun's energy.
That left glaciers vulnerable to melting even faster in subsequent heatwaves.
"Ten years ago, I wouldn't have thought that it's possible to lose glaciers so quickly," said Dr Fabien Maussion, a glaciologist at the University of Bristol, who was not involved in the Swiss report.
"What's happened over the summer now is extremely distressingâ¦ but at the same time it was to be expected from a climate scientist's perspective," he added.
Meltwater from glaciers can be an important source of water for irrigation, hydropower and even shipping traffic during hot, dry conditions.
Scientists estimate that Swiss glaciers released 2.2 trillion litres of meltwater between July and September.
Although that helped to ease water shortages this summer, it has rapidly diminished the frozen supply.
The loss of ice could pose long-term challenges, Huss warned, with smaller glaciers unable to top up water levels to the same extent.
"Every drop of water that runs off during these heatwaves is kind of old water that's been stocked in the glacier ice centuries or decades ago," said Huss.
"It's helping us [now] but it's unsustainable, so we won't have it at [our] disposal in the next heatwave."
The River Rhine reached record lows in places this summer , affecting shipping navigation routes and increasing transport costs.
One of the most ominous findings is what researchers observed at measurement sites at the highest elevations, where temperatures are lowest and glaciers are typically snow-covered.
Even as high as 3,500 metres above sea level, scientists found no snow remaining at the end of summer.
"At some glaciers we've seen four metres of ice loss at the highest point, where they should be covered by several metres of winter snow at this time of the year," said Huss, from Glacier Monitoring Switzerland.
Snow is like glacier food - and under stable conditions some of it would eventually compact into ice.
But if no snow survives the summer, it cannot replace the ice lost to melting at lower, warmer elevations. The glacier will starve, shrink and eventually disappear.
"Glaciers are complex because they gain mass at the top and they flow downstream, so there is a lot of physics," explained Maussion.
"But in its simplest form, what we see right now is that we took an ice cube out of the fridge and it's just melting in front of our eyes."
Scientists say the climate is now too warm for many Alpine glaciers to survive.
Some, like Plattalva in eastern Switzerland, have already disappeared.
But researchers stress that sharp cuts to carbon emissions can still save much of the world's glacier ice.
This is particularly the case for the Himalayas and the polar regions, where most of the planet's ice resides.
"There we still can make a big difference with protecting the climate," said Huss.
"If these ice masses can be saved or stabilised, we can limit the rise of global sea levelsâ¦ which could affect billions of people living along the coast."

articles.content_orig:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declined an invitation to appear at a Senate subcommittee hearing on Wednesday on the risks of rogue artificial intelligence , according to Sen. Josh Hawley , R-Mo.
Hawley, who chairs the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs subpanel that held the hearing, sent a letter to Altman on Sept. 25 requesting his presence to "help shed light on the Subcommittee's ongoing investigation into recent rogue AI incidents involving OpenAI models." NBC News first reported that Altman did not accept the invitation to testify.
"He turned us down," Hawley said of Altman at the hearing. "I think that's unfortunate because I think the American people deserve to know exactly what's going on at all of these companies. And to give us the sort of transparency that I think is needed for not just comfort, but to have an understanding of what these companies — that are the most powerful companies in the world — are doing right now with the most powerful technology ever known to man."
A spokesperson for OpenAI noted that Altman received the invitation to testify on Friday, just five days ahead of the hearing. Altman on Tuesday appeared at the company's annual DevDay developer conference in San Francisco as other AI officials — including OpenAI President Greg Brockman — were in Washington meeting with President Donald Trump.
"OpenAI is deeply engaged with Congress on federal policies to advance AI safety, including through dozens of meetings in recent weeks with members of both parties in both chambers," the spokesperson said. "We look forward to continuing to work constructively and proactively with Senator Hawley and members of Congress on federal AI safety legislation that materially raises the safety bar."
Hawley's overture to Altman comes weeks after he opened an investigation into OpenAI earlier this month. Hawley sought information on a cyberattack involving hundreds of OpenAI agents that broke out of their testing sandbox and hacked into the systems of another AI company called Hugging Face.
The cyber attack was one in a series of recent hacks involving frontier AI models that have raised alarms and prompted calls for Congress to act to rein in the rapidly evolving technology.
Hawley requested information from Altman on the cyber attack and on the existential risks of the technology and set an Oct. 1 deadline. A spokesperson for Hawley said OpenAI is expected to provide additional documents by the end of the week.
"The American people deserve to know the details of what went on in the Hugging Face incident and other incidents of AI models going rogue.  This investigation will seek those answers," Hawley said in the Sept. 10 letter.
